result.summary: Minerva warns Telemachus to leave Sparta, and after receiving gifts from Menelaus and Helen he sails home, taking the exiled seer Theoclymenus aboard at Pylos. Meanwhile Eumaeus tells Ulysses how he was stolen from Syra as a child and sold to Laertes. Telemachus lands in Ithaca and heads for the swineherd's hut.

scenes.title: Minerva's warning at Sparta
scenes.summary: Minerva tells Telemachus to hurry home and avoid the suitors' ambush. Pisistratus urges him to wait for morning and the host's gifts.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus risks ambush and the loss of his property and perhaps his mother's remarriage.

scenes.title: Gifts and omen from Menelaus
scenes.summary: Menelaus and Helen give Telemachus gifts and a farewell meal. An eagle with a goose appears, and Helen reads it as Ulysses' coming revenge.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus wants to return before his property is lost.

scenes.title: Journey to Pylos and the ship
scenes.summary: They stay at Pherae, then reach Pylos. Telemachus has Pisistratus leave him at the ship so Nestor cannot delay him.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus fears delay while danger waits at home.

scenes.title: Theoclymenus joins the voyage
scenes.summary: The seer Theoclymenus, a fugitive killer, asks for passage. His ancestry is recounted and Telemachus takes him aboard and sails.
scenes.stakes: Theoclymenus faces death at the hands of his victim's kinsmen.

scenes.title: Ulysses tests Eumaeus
scenes.summary: Ulysses says he will go beg in town. Eumaeus dissuades him and tells of Laertes and Anticlea.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks losing his shelter and exposing himself to the suitors.

scenes.title: Eumaeus's tale of Syra
scenes.summary: Eumaeus tells how a Phoenician nurse and traders kidnapped him from Syra. The woman died at sea and he was sold to Laertes.
scenes.stakes: As a child Eumaeus was stolen from his home and family.

scenes.title: Telemachus lands in Ithaca
scenes.summary: Telemachus lands, entrusts Theoclymenus to Piraeus, and reads another omen. He walks to Eumaeus's farm.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus must avoid the suitors' ambush.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses rosy-fingered Dawn and Aurora for the dawn goddess.

notable_quotes.reason: Menelaus's maxim on moderation in hospitality.
Eumaeus says suffering is pleasant to recall afterwards.

analysis.text: Hospitality shapes the book: Menelaus's measured generosity and Eumaeus's kindness contrast with the suitors' abuse.
Omens and prophecy point toward Ulysses' return and the suitors' fall.

legacy.text: Eumaeus's line that a man who has suffered enjoys recalling past sorrows became a much quoted sentiment, echoed in the Latin 'forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit'.

fun_facts.text: Eumaeus's tale of Phoenician kidnappers reflects the Phoenicians' reputation as sea traders in early Greek poetry.

language_notes.text: "A fool's errand" means a journey that achieves nothing; Telemachus's trip would be wasted if the suitors consume his estate.
"Dead and done with" is blunt: a dead husband is no longer remembered by a remarrying wife. Minerva voices a cynical generalization.
The Strait between Ithaca and Samos is the narrow channel where the suitors have set an ambush; Samos here is the island also called Same.
"Yoke the horses" means harness them to the chariot.
Guest-gifts were customary; a host gave presents and a formal farewell, so leaving without them would break the rules of hospitality.
Menelaus states a rule of hospitality: a host should neither keep a guest against his will nor push him out when he wishes to stay.
Hellas and the Peloponnese here mean Greece proper and its southern peninsula; Menelaus offers a tour of the main cities.
A tripod is a three-legged bronze cauldron or stand, a valued gift and a typical mark of wealth in Homeric society.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the divine smith, so the bowl is a godlike masterwork of the highest value.
The Sidonians were Phoenicians from Sidon, famed as craftsmen and traders; Menelaus got the bowl on his long wanderings home from Troy.
A drink-offering is a libation: wine poured to the gods for a safe journey.
Birds flying on the right were lucky omens in Greek belief; an eagle was Jove's bird and often signified his will.
The horses 'swayed the yoke' by pulling the chariot; the yoke is the wooden beam across the horses' necks, so the phrasing is loose and poetic.
The text seems to omit a verb: they yoked the horses and 'their places in the chariot' means they took their places in the chariot.
'Nothing loath' means quite willing; the horses ran eagerly without needing to be urged.
'The warmth of his good will' means Nestor's kindly, eager hospitality, which would keep Telemachus from leaving.
'Raiment' means clothing; 'deemed' means judged or considered.
Melampus was jailed by Phylacus for trying to drive off the cattle of Phylacus' house, which Neleus' daughter's suitor needed; the 'daughter of Neleus' is Pero, whom he sought for his brother Bias.
Erinys: a Fury, a goddess of vengeance who punishes wrongdoing; here she sends a madness or sorrow upon Melampus.
Swearing 'by your own head' was a solemn way of appealing to someone, treating their life as the pledge of truthfulness.
Suppliant: someone who humbly asks protection, which Greek custom and Jove obliged hosts to grant.
Forestays are ropes running from the mast top to the bow, steadying the mast; the sheets are ropes controlling the sails.
The 'flying islands' are the Echinades off western Greece; the footnote number 132 is an editorial marker. Telemachus fears the suitors' ambush near Ithaca.
"Prove" here means test or put to the proof, not demonstrate.
"As I needs must" is archaic for "as I must of necessity"; begging is his only means of living.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) was god of luck, gain and skilful service, so Ulysses invokes him as patron of handy work.
"Miserable bellies" means that hunger drives poor men to endure hardship; the stomach is blamed for their wandering.
"Threshold of old age" is a figure for the start of old age; Laertes was already ageing when his son left.
Hades here means the house of the god of the dead, the underworld where the dead dwell.
The stray "133" is a footnote marker from the printed edition, not part of the story.
Same is an island kingdom near Ithaca; the family of Ctimene's husband gave a bride-price or dowry exchange in marriage.
Syra and Ortygia are vaguely placed islands; Ortygia is often linked with Delos. The 'turning' of the land suggests the island lies at a far edge of the known world.
Sudden, painless death was attributed to Apollo (men) and Diana (women), the archer gods, whose arrows ('shafts') bring gentle death in old age.
'Gewgaws' are showy trinkets of little real value, the kind of goods traders used to tempt buyers.
Taphians were seafaring raiders known for piracy and slave-taking, who lived on islands off western Greece.
'Keep your own counsel' means keep the plan secret and tell no one.
'Sundry of his chattels' means various items of his movable property, i.e. Laertes paid for Eumaeus with goods.
"Mooring stones" were heavy stones dropped as anchors; the hawsers are the ropes that secure the ship to shore.
"Repair" here means to go or resort to a place, not to fix something.
"Wooer" means suitor; "paying court" means courting Penelope, here in the hope of marrying her and becoming master of Ulysses' house.
A hawk was sacred to Apollo, god of prophecy, so a hawk on the right was read as a favourable sign from him.
"Doughty" is archaic for strong and sturdy.

context_notes.text: Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' protector and has guided Telemachus throughout his journey. Lacedaemon is Sparta, Menelaus's kingdom.
Eurymachus is one of the leading suitors of Penelope. Her family's pressure to remarry reflects the customs of the time, in which a woman's father and brothers could arrange her marriage.
The swineherd is Eumaeus, Ulysses' loyal servant, whose hut Telemachus will visit first, as the next scenes show.
Helen's own handiwork recalls her role as a weaver in the Iliad. Giving it shows her gracious standing in Sparta after Troy.
Helen gives the robe for Telemachus' future bride, a traditional wedding gift.
Nestor of Pylos hosted Telemachus first; he fought beside Menelaus at Troy, so Menelaus sends thanks back to him.
Pherae was a town on the road between Sparta and Pylos. Diocles, its lord, had also hosted Telemachus on the outward journey.
Telemachus's father Ulysses and Pisistratus's father Nestor fought together at Troy, which is the 'old friendship' he invokes. Telemachus fears delay while suitors plot against him.
A seer was a prophet who read signs from gods. Killing a kinsman forced the killer into exile to escape blood vengeance.
Amphiaraus, a seer, was betrayed by his wife Eriphyle, who accepted a necklace as a bribe, and died fighting at Thebes.
Aurora is the dawn goddess (the Greek Eos), who in myth often carried off beautiful mortal men.
Taking a guest's spear and stowing it was a courtesy that marked his acceptance as a guest.
Ulysses is disguised as a beggar, so he speaks of himself in the third person to Eumaeus, who does not recognise him.
The suitors had taken over Ulysses' house, feasting on his goods and keeping young, well-dressed servants.
Laertes is Ulysses' father and Anticlea his mother; she died of grief over her absent son.
Phoenicians, from the Levant coast, were famed sea traders in Homeric poetry, and often shown as cunning and dishonest.
Sidon was a major Phoenician city. The woman claims noble, wealthy origins, which makes her enslavement more pitiable.
Laertes is Ulysses' father, so Eumaeus was bought into the household of Ulysses' own family, though Ulysses is hiding his identity.
Penelope avoids the suitors by staying in her upper chamber. Eurymachus is one of the leading suitors, though Telemachus speaks of him as respected.
Theoclymenus is a seer who fled his homeland after a killing. Telemachus took him aboard as a suppliant, so he needs a host in Ithaca.

literary_notes.text: Pisistratus sleeps soundly while Telemachus lies awake worrying, which shows the prince's anxious devotion to his absent father.
Minerva's cynical remark about women plays on Telemachus's fears and makes him hurry, and quietly contrasts with the faithful Penelope.
Minerva predicts that the suitors will die instead of Telemachus, hinting at the poem's eventual outcome.
Pisistratus's maxim restates the Odyssey's central value of hospitality (xenia), here as courtesy toward a generous host.
Menelaus' balanced maxim shows him as a courteous, thoughtful host who values proper measure.
The robe glittering like a star conveys its great beauty and brightness.
The eagle stands for Ulysses, and the seized goose for the suitors who prey on his household.
Helen's reading of the omen predicts Ulysses' return and vengeance on the suitors, which the story will fulfil.
'Rosy-fingered Dawn' is a Homeric formula that marks the start of a new day and recurs throughout the poem.
Pisistratus's remark about his father's obstinacy gives a brief, affectionate portrait of Nestor as a hospitable old man who insists on his way.
Pisistratus's prediction that Nestor will be angry and come to the ship hints at the urgency of Telemachus's departure and the pressure on him.
'Throned in gold' is a stock description of Aurora, typical of Homeric formulaic phrases.
Telemachus' firm, honest answer shows his growing confidence, though he speaks of Ulysses as probably dead.
Minerva's help with a favourable wind repeats the recurring theme of divine guidance protecting Telemachus.
His worry about death or capture hints at the suitors' planned ambush.
The narrator openly states Ulysses' hidden motive, so we know his offer is a test rather than a real plan.
Ulysses offers news of himself to Penelope while Eumaeus does not know the beggar is her husband.
The suitors' pride reaching "the very heavens" stresses how extreme their arrogance is.
Eumaeus' fond memory of being raised beside Ctimene shows his loyalty, gratitude and warmth toward the household.
Eumaeus voices a general truth about suffering and memory, which frames the story and invites Ulysses, who has suffered much, to share it.
The woman's sudden fall into the hold is compared to a sea gull dropping onto water, making her death swift and limp, and tied to Diana's arrow.
Ulysses consoles Eumaeus as a beggar while the audience knows he is the master Eumaeus serves, and that his own wandering is nearly over.
Telemachus says Jove alone knows whether the suitors will come to a bad end, and the audience knows they will.
The hawk tearing the dove symbolizes the strong overcoming the weak, which Theoclymenus reads as Telemachus's house prevailing over its rivals.
"The excellent swineherd" and his devoted service prepare for Eumaeus's loyalty, which matters in later books.
